title: Revolutionary Generosity
subtitle: How Families Give While They Live, Give More Than Cash, and Leave More Than Money
status: Concept outline — prepared for discussion. Not an approved project of The Signatry.

parts.name: Who Owns This?
parts.premise: The inner work. Before a family can give differently it has to answer an ownership question, and then face the fear that has been quietly answering it for years.

parts.name: What You Actually Own
parts.premise: The mechanics almost no one is taught. Where the wealth actually sits, why timing decides the size of a gift, and how a giving trajectory replaces the annual argument.

parts.name: The Family Is the Unit
parts.premise: Generosity is not inherited, it is rehearsed. Inheritance design, family decision-making, and the transfer that is currently being handled entirely by attorneys.

parts.name: The Company You Keep
parts.premise: No one gives well alone. The rooms, tables, advisors, and churches that either produce generous families or quietly prevent them.

parts.name: What It's All For
parts.premise: Outcomes and the end of the matter. How to keep score, what to aim at, who is actually teaching whom, and the return that makes the whole thing worth it.

chapters.title: The Deed, Not the Feeling
chapters.premise: Stewardship is not a posture toward money. It is a change of ownership that has to happen somewhere a person can point to. Most Christians affirm that God owns it all and then manage as owners anyway, which is why every act of giving feels like subtraction.
chapters.anchor: Ron Blue's lifelong argument that God owns it all, read as a legal and practical claim rather than a devotional one.
chapters.story: An owner who signed something — a document, a trust, a first significant gift — and can name the date. Steve's own moment of realignment after the sale belongs near here, told plainly.
chapters.turn: The question stops being "how generous am I?" and becomes "on whose behalf am I managing this?"
chapters.action: Write the sentence "I am managing ______ on behalf of ______" and put a date on it.
chapters.magnet: Stewardship isn't a mood. Until ownership actually changes hands — in a document, a decision, a date you can name — every gift will feel like subtraction. The people who give freely are the ones who stopped managing their own money years ago.
chapters.question: On whose behalf am I managing this — and when did that change?

chapters.title: Your Heart Follows Your Money
chapters.premise: People wait to feel generous before they give. Jesus says the treasure moves first and the heart follows after it. That makes giving a means of formation rather than evidence of it.
chapters.anchor: Randy Alcorn's reading of Matthew 6:21 — "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (NIV).
chapters.story: Someone who gave before they wanted to, and what had changed in them a year later.
chapters.turn: Generosity is not the final exam. It is the curriculum.
chapters.action: Give one gift this month that is larger than your current affection justifies.
chapters.magnet: Most people wait to feel generous before they give. Jesus says it runs the other way — the treasure moves first, and the heart follows it. Generosity isn't the final exam. It's the curriculum.
chapters.question: What would I have to give for my heart to follow it somewhere new?

chapters.title: It Was Never Greed
chapters.premise: Almost nobody withholds because they love money. They withhold because they are afraid — of running out, of a market, of a child's future, of looking foolish. Naming fear as the real opponent changes the entire conversation, and rescues generous people from a guilt that never produced generosity anyway.
chapters.anchor: The contentment thread running through Ron Blue's counsel, and the language of surrender April Chapman uses about generosity beginning with an emptied hand.
chapters.story: A couple who could easily afford to give and didn't, told with enough sympathy that the reader recognizes himself before he judges them.
chapters.turn: The reader stops feeling guilty and starts being honest, which is the only place change has ever begun.
chapters.action: Name the fear in one sentence. Then name the smallest gift that would test it.
chapters.magnet: Almost no one withholds because they love money. They withhold because they are afraid — of running out, of a market, of a child's future. Guilt has never produced a generous person. Naming the fear has.
chapters.question: What exactly am I afraid of, and what is the smallest gift that would test it?

chapters.title: How Much Is Enough?
chapters.premise: A family that never sets a ceiling will spend forty years negotiating a floor. Naming a financial finish line converts every dollar above it from an annual debate into an assignment.
chapters.anchor: April Chapman's inversion of the giving question, and Ron Blue's counsel on defining what is enough.
chapters.story: A family that named a number — what it cost them to say it out loud, and what it freed.
chapters.turn: The tithe is a floor argument. The finish line is a ceiling argument, and ceilings are what actually free people.
chapters.action: Draft your number this quarter. Tell one person outside your family what it is.
chapters.magnet: A family that never sets a ceiling will spend forty years negotiating a floor. The tithe is a floor argument. The finish line is a ceiling argument — and it's the ceiling that sets people free.
chapters.question: What is our number, and who besides us knows it?

chapters.title: The Checkbook Is the Smallest Room in the House
chapters.premise: The overwhelming majority of American wealth sits outside cash — in businesses, land, appreciated securities, crops, equipment, intellectual property — while the overwhelming majority of giving comes out of the checking account. That mismatch is the largest unclaimed opportunity in Christian philanthropy, and it has nothing to do with income.
chapters.anchor: The asset-based giving practice built by National Christian Foundation and carried into The Signatry's core work.
chapters.story: A giver whose annual gift moved from four figures to seven without a dollar of change in income, because the gift came from an asset instead of a paycheck.
chapters.turn: I am not a small giver. I have been giving out of the smallest account I own.
chapters.action: List every asset you own that is not cash. Circle the one you would be least sorry to part with.
chapters.magnet: Most wealth in America isn't cash — it's businesses, land, stock, equipment, intellectual property. Most giving is cash. That single mismatch is the largest unclaimed opportunity in Christian philanthropy, and it has nothing to do with income.
chapters.question: What do I own that I have never once considered giving?

chapters.title: Two Weeks Too Late
chapters.premise: A gift of ownership made before a letter of intent is worth dramatically more to the Kingdom than a gift of proceeds made after the wire clears. The difference is entirely sequence, and most owners learn it after the closing, from an advisor who assumed they weren't interested.
chapters.anchor: Steve's own exit, and the business-owner practice at the center of The Signatry's work with closely held companies.
chapters.story: Two owners, the same company value, opposite sequence. Told as a story rather than a spreadsheet, so the reader feels the cost of the conversation that never happened.
chapters.turn: The most generous decision of your life may have a deadline you don't know about.
chapters.action: If a sale is even possible within five years, have the conversation now — not with a broker, with someone who does this.
chapters.magnet: A gift of ownership made before a letter of intent is worth vastly more to the Kingdom than a gift of proceeds made after the wire clears. The difference is timing. Most owners learn it two weeks too late.
chapters.question: Is there a transaction in my future with a generosity deadline I have never calendared?

chapters.title: Give While You Live
chapters.premise: Giving at death is a transaction. Giving during life is a discipleship — you see the outcome, correct your mistakes, learn what you fund well, and your children watch you do it.
chapters.anchor: David Green's decision to move ownership of the company beyond the family's reach, and the giving-while-living conviction he has argued for since.
chapters.story: A father who gave a significant asset away in front of his adult children, and what those children did with their own money ten years later.
chapters.turn: An estate plan teaches nothing. A parent who gave in daylight teaches everything.
chapters.action: Move one gift you had planned for your estate into the next twelve months.
chapters.magnet: Giving at death is a transaction. Giving during life is a discipleship — you see the outcome, correct your mistakes, and your children watch you do it. An estate plan teaches nothing. A parent giving in daylight teaches everything.
chapters.question: What am I planning to give after I die that I could give while they can still watch?

chapters.title: The Ladder
chapters.premise: A one-time gift is an event. An escalating percentage is a life. Raising the number every year removes the annual negotiation that exhausts most couples, and it handles the windfall before the windfall arrives.
chapters.anchor: Rick Warren's long practice of increasing his own giving percentage year over year rather than settling at a figure.
chapters.story: A couple twenty years into a ladder, and what year seven felt like — the year it stopped being comfortable.
chapters.turn: You do not need more money to become generous. You need a slope.
chapters.action: Write down this year's percentage and next year's. Put both somewhere you will see them in December.
chapters.magnet: A one-time gift is an event. An escalating percentage is a life. Raise the number every year and you stop negotiating every December — and you're ready when the windfall shows up.
chapters.question: What is our percentage this year, and what will it be next year?

chapters.title: One Generous Parent Is Not a Legacy
chapters.premise: Philanthropy speaks in individuals; Scripture and inheritance both operate on households. A family that decides together produces adult children who give. A family with one generous parent and four silent heirs produces litigation.
chapters.anchor: The across-generations mandate at the center of The Signatry's mission, and Bill High's insistence that family story — not only structure — is what actually carries.
chapters.story: Two families with comparable balance sheets and opposite outcomes at the reading of the will.
chapters.turn: Generosity is not inherited. It is rehearsed.
chapters.action: Hold one family meeting this year in which the children decide where a real amount goes.
chapters.magnet: Philanthropy speaks in individuals. Scripture and inheritance both operate on households. Generosity is not inherited — it's rehearsed. A family that decides together raises adult children who give.
chapters.question: When did our children last decide where real money went?

chapters.title: Equal Isn't Always Fair
chapters.premise: Dividing an estate evenly is often the lazy choice rather than the loving one. How you transfer assets to children is a parenting decision with a long tail, and the explanation belongs to you — delivered while everyone is alive to discuss it.
chapters.anchor: Ron Blue's work on inheritance, and the distinction between what an heir could receive and what would actually help.
chapters.story: A family that divided unequally, said why out loud, and remained a family.
chapters.turn: The goal is not to be fair to your children. It is to be wise about them.
chapters.action: Write the letter that explains your decisions. Read it to them yourself.
chapters.magnet: Dividing an estate evenly is often the lazy choice rather than the loving one. The question isn't what each child could receive — it's what amount would actually help. And the explanation belongs to you, delivered while you can still give it.
chapters.question: Have I confused being fair with being wise?

chapters.title: The Largest Discipleship Opportunity of Our Lifetime
chapters.premise: Tens of trillions of dollars are moving between generations over the next two decades. Nearly all of the professional energy aimed at it concerns tax and preservation. Almost none concerns whether the values survive the transfer.
chapters.anchor: The generational mandate at the center of The Signatry's mission, and the legacy training built around it.
chapters.story: An heir who received everything and understood nothing — told with sympathy rather than judgment, because it was not his fault.
chapters.turn: The transfer is not a tax event. It is a discipleship event currently being handled entirely by attorneys.
chapters.action: Ask your estate attorney what the plan teaches your children. Sit through the silence.
chapters.magnet: Tens of trillions of dollars are moving between generations, and nearly all the professional energy around it concerns tax and preservation. Almost none concerns whether the values survive the transfer.
chapters.question: What does our estate plan teach our children about God?

chapters.title: Friction Is Not Neutral
chapters.premise: People rarely fail to be generous for lack of conviction. They fail because the path from asset to impact is slow, complicated, expensive, and staffed by people paid on what stays. Design quietly redirects generosity into accumulation.
chapters.anchor: The counter-design behind The Signatry's own fund structure — no asset-based fees, no minimums, and a grant rate well above the industry norm. Handled as a principle, with the mechanics in the appendix.
chapters.story: A giver who tried to give an illiquid asset the hard way, waited nine months, and gave up.
chapters.turn: Souls are downstream of defaults.
chapters.action: Audit your own giving path. Count the steps between the decision and the delivery.
chapters.magnet: People rarely fail to be generous for lack of conviction. They fail because the path from asset to impact is slow, expensive, and staffed by people paid on what stays. Friction is not neutral — it quietly redirects generosity into accumulation.
chapters.question: How many steps stand between my decision to give and the gift arriving?

chapters.title: The Room Where No One Wants Anything
chapters.premise: Wealthy Christians spend their lives being handled. The single environment that reliably produces candor is the one where nobody is permitted to ask, which is precisely why the Journey of Generosity works.
chapters.anchor: Generous Giving's founding discipline — privately funded since 2000 so that it never has to solicit and never tells anyone where to give.
chapters.story: The last hour of a JOG, told by someone who arrived defended and left different.
chapters.turn: The absence of the ask is not politeness. It is the entire method.
chapters.action: Sit in one room this year where nobody wants anything from you. Then host one.
chapters.magnet: Wealthy Christians spend their lives being handled. The one room that produces honesty is the room where nobody is allowed to ask for anything. The absence of the ask isn't politeness — it's the method.
chapters.question: When was I last in a room about money where no one wanted anything from me?

chapters.title: Nobody Gives Well Alone
chapters.premise: Generous families do their best work in the company of other generous families. Solo philanthropy drifts toward the sentimental or the defensive; a table of peers asks harder questions and funds harder problems.
chapters.anchor: The convening model The Gathering has built among Christian givers under Josh Kwan's leadership.
chapters.story: A funding decision that was materially improved — or mercifully prevented — by one peer at a table.
chapters.turn: The more common condition among the wealthy is not stinginess. It is loneliness.
chapters.action: Find or convene four families who will meet twice a year and show each other their giving.
chapters.magnet: Generous families do their best work in the company of other generous families. Solo giving drifts toward the sentimental or the defensive; a table of peers asks harder questions. The more common condition among the wealthy isn't stinginess — it's loneliness.
chapters.question: Who sees my giving and is allowed to question it?

chapters.title: The Question That Never Got Asked
chapters.premise: Most charitable intent in America dies quietly in a professional's office because no one raised the subject — out of fear of seeming to sell something, or an assumption that faith is private. The advisor who asks well does not lose assets. He gains trust, referrals, and the next two generations of the family.
chapters.anchor: The advisor channel built over two decades by Kingdom Advisors, and the advisor-facing practice at The Signatry.
chapters.story: An advisor who asked one question and watched a twenty-year relationship change shape.
chapters.turn: The gate to the largest generosity in America is a professional who is afraid of seeming to sell something.
chapters.action: If you are a client, raise it yourself. If you are an advisor, ask it this week. Written so a client can be handed this chapter without embarrassment.
chapters.magnet: Most charitable intent in America dies quietly in a professional's office because nobody raised the subject. The advisor who asks doesn't lose assets — he gains trust, referrals, and the next two generations of the family.
chapters.question: Has anyone who advises me ever asked what I want my money to do?

chapters.title: Stop Talking About Money Only When You Need Some
chapters.premise: Churches that discuss giving only during budget season train congregations to hear every mention of money as an ask, and to defend themselves accordingly. Taught as formation, generosity frees people. Taught as fundraising, it hardens them.
chapters.anchor: The purpose-driven conviction that giving is worship and discipleship rather than institutional maintenance.
chapters.story: A pastor who preached a generosity series with no offering attached, and what happened in the year that followed.
chapters.turn: Giving usually rises — and if that is why you did it, you have already lost the thing you were after.
chapters.action: Preach or host one series on generosity with nothing attached to it.
chapters.magnet: Churches that discuss money only when they need some train their people to hear every mention of giving as an ask. Taught as formation, generosity frees people. Taught as fundraising, it hardens them.
chapters.question: When did our church last talk about money without needing any?

chapters.title: Measure the Outflow
chapters.premise: Every financial institution in the world reports how much it holds. A Kingdom institution should report how fast money leaves, and publish it annually. That single change in scorekeeping implicates the reader as much as the industry.
chapters.anchor: The grant-velocity standard The Signatry has adopted against an industry norm built on assets under management.
chapters.story: A fund that sat untouched for a decade, and the family that finally opened it.
chapters.turn: A donor advised fund that never grants is a savings account with better tax treatment and worse theology.
chapters.action: Calculate what percentage of your fund left this year. Set next year's target and tell someone.
chapters.magnet: Every financial institution reports what it holds. A Kingdom institution should report how fast money leaves. A fund that never grants is a savings account with better tax treatment and worse theology.
chapters.question: What percentage of what we set aside for God actually left this year?

chapters.title: From Charity to Problem-Solving
chapters.premise: Funding whatever letter arrives is generous. Choosing one problem and staying with it for a decade is something else, and it requires the giver to say what winning would look like — which is exactly where most philanthropy quietly declines to go.
chapters.anchor: The Signatry's stated aim of solving the world's greatest problems, and the strategic philanthropy practiced across the movement.
chapters.story: A family that picked one problem and stayed with it long enough to be surprised by what worked.
chapters.turn: Strategy is a way of loving more. It is never a permission slip to give later.
chapters.action: Name one problem you intend to still be funding in ten years.
chapters.magnet: Funding whatever letter arrives is generous. Choosing one problem and staying with it for a decade is something else — and it requires you to say what winning looks like. Strategy is a way of loving more, never a reason to give later.
chapters.question: What problem will we still be funding in ten years?

chapters.title: It Isn't an American Idea
chapters.premise: Generosity movements have taken root in Brazil, India, Kenya and elsewhere, often faster and with less baggage than at home. That matters theologically, because it proves this conviction is not a byproduct of surplus.
chapters.anchor: Daryl Heald's work planting generosity movements outside the United States.
chapters.story: A giver in a poor country whose ordinary practice both indicts and instructs a giver in a rich one.
chapters.turn: You are not the teacher in this movement. You may well be the student.
chapters.action: Fund something you cannot supervise, and let someone else decide how it is spent.
chapters.magnet: Generosity movements have taken root in Brazil, India, and Kenya — often faster and with less baggage than in the United States. This is not a byproduct of surplus. And the giver in the poorer country is usually the one teaching.
chapters.question: Whose generosity would humble me if I saw it up close?

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.premise: The giver is the primary beneficiary. The joy is real rather than compensatory, and a family that lives this way is running the most persuasive argument for the gospel available to it. The last trap is the applause — the joy belongs to people who stopped needing their name on the building.
chapters.anchor: Todd Harper's two decades of arguing that joy is the actual return, and April Chapman's conviction that generosity is among the strongest evangelism the church has.
chapters.story: End on a face rather than a balance sheet — a giver late in life who would not trade any of it back.
chapters.turn: If the reader closes the book calculating, the book failed. If he closes it wanting, it worked.
chapters.action: Give one gift this year that no one will ever know about.
chapters.magnet: The giver is the primary beneficiary. The joy is real, not compensatory — and a family living this way is running the most persuasive argument for the gospel available to them. End on a face, not a balance sheet.
chapters.question: What will I give this year that no one will ever know about?
